setup: This is the story of a city told almost entirely by the people who destroyed it. Carthage wrote extensively — histories, science, religion, an agricultural literature the Romans admired — and almost none of it survives, because when Rome burned the city in 146 BCE it dispersed or destroyed the entire written record. So everything here comes filtered through Greek and Roman sources: the very people who fought Carthage for centuries and finally erased it. Keep that in mind throughout. The chapter opens with the founding, around 814 BCE, when a Tyrian princess named Elissa (the Romans called her Dido) fled her brother's murder of her husband and sailed west from the great Phoenician port of Tyre to plant a colony on the North African coast. She named it Qart Hadasht — the New City. The location was the whole point: it sat astride the narrowest pinch of the central Mediterranean, the toll booth on the busiest sea-lane in the ancient world. What is at stake is whether a dependent outpost can outgrow its mother city and become a power in its own right.

bridge: Chapter 1 founded Carthage around 814 BCE as a Tyrian colony on the African coast, sitting astride the central Mediterranean chokepoint. As its mother city Tyre buckled under Neo-Assyrian pressure, the colony grew independent, and by roughly 700 BCE Carthage was the dominant Phoenician city in the west — rich, heavily fortified, worshipping its own gods Baal Hammon and Tanit. But it was still essentially a trading city that fought only when it had to. That was about to change.
setup: Around 580 BCE a general named Mago I seizes power and founds the Magonid dynasty, and under his family Carthage stops thinking of itself as a trading city that occasionally fights and starts thinking of itself as a military power that trades. The driver is competition: Greek colonists have been pouring into Sicily and southern Italy for two centuries, and the old live-and-let-live arrangement with the Phoenicians is breaking down as both sides reach for the same harbors and trade routes. Mago professionalizes the army, expands the navy, and allies with the Etruscans of central Italy, who are being squeezed by the same Greeks. The contest will be decided at sea and on the islands between Africa and Italy. At the same time, the most astonishing Carthaginian achievements of the era are not battles at all but two voyages into the open Atlantic — south into tropical Africa and north toward the tin of Britain — waters no other Mediterranean people dared. The question is whether Carthage can wall the Greeks out of the western sea.

bridge: Chapter 2 turned Carthage into a military power under the Magonid dynasty, divided the western Mediterranean with the Greeks, and sent its explorers down the African coast and up toward Britain. It ended with the last great Magonid, Hamilcar I, preparing a massive invasion of eastern Sicily and the Greek world centered on Syracuse — the confrontation both sides knew was coming. In 480 BCE it came, and it was a catastrophe.
setup: In the same year the Greeks broke the Persian navy at Salamis, Hamilcar I's army is routed at Himera in Sicily and Hamilcar himself is killed. The defeat knocks Carthage out of Sicilian warfare for seventy years — but instead of collapsing, Carthage pivots, and the pivot produces its most remarkable century. The Magonid dynasty falls, replaced by a mixed republic of elected magistrates, a council, and an assembly so well-balanced that the Greek philosopher Aristotle ranked it among the best-governed states in the world. Blocked from Sicily, Carthage turns inward and southward, conquering the African interior, covering the land with agricultural estates that make it one of the ancient world's great grain exporters, and reaching across the Sahara for gold. It also builds the Cothon, a circular military harbor that could shelter 220 warships, an engineering marvel with no ancient equal. The Sicilian wars never quite end — they simmer through a grinding century of invasion, siege, and plague. What is at stake is whether a defeated power can reinvent itself into something stronger.

bridge: Across the last three chapters Carthage grew from a Tyrian colony into the master of the western Mediterranean: a wealthy republic praised by Aristotle, an African empire feeding on grain and Saharan gold, a navy with no equal sheltered in the great circular Cothon. Its long enemies had been the Greeks of Sicily, fought to a grinding stalemate over two centuries. One power it had barely noticed was Rome — back in 509 BCE Carthage signed a treaty treating the young republic as a minor neighbor controlling a few hundred square miles of farmland. That was about to become the most expensive miscalculation in its history.
setup: In 264 BCE a petty dispute over the Sicilian town of Messana drags Carthage and Rome into a war neither planned — the First Punic War, which will run twenty-three years and become the longest continuous conflict in ancient history to that point. The problem is geography: to fight over Sicily, an island, the war must be won at sea, and Carthage has the finest navy in the western Mediterranean while Rome, in 264 BCE, has no navy at all. By every rational measure it should be over quickly. But the Romans turn out to be constitutionally incapable of accepting defeat. They reverse-engineer a captured Carthaginian warship, build a fleet from scratch, and bolt on a crude boarding bridge that turns sea battles into infantry fights — neutralizing everything the Carthaginians are good at. What is at stake is naval supremacy over the western sea, and behind it, which of these two cities will dominate the Mediterranean.

bridge: Chapter 4 ended in disaster. After twenty-three years, Carthage lost the First Punic War, surrendered Sicily, and went bankrupt paying Rome's indemnity. Then its unpaid mercenaries revolted in the savage Truceless War that nearly destroyed the state — and while Carthage fought for survival, Rome seized Sardinia and Corsica in an act even the pro-Roman Polybius called naked opportunism. The one man whose reputation came out of all this enhanced was Hamilcar Barca, the general who had been undefeated in Sicily and who crushed the mercenary revolt. And Hamilcar was already thinking about the next war.
setup: In 237 BCE Hamilcar Barca crosses to Iberia — modern Spain and Portugal — and brings his nine-year-old son Hannibal, who, by a story the sources repeat, swears an oath at the altar of Baal Hammon: eternal enmity against Rome. This is not ordinary empire-building. It is a revenge operation, designed from the start to build the army and the money for a second war. The key is silver: Iberia sits on some of the richest silver deposits in the ancient world, and Hamilcar seizes the mines with the focus of a mining executive, funding a professional army loyal to his family rather than to the Carthaginian Senate back home — a Barcid kingdom-within-a-state thousands of miles from the oligarchs who are supposed to control it. Hamilcar dies, his son-in-law Hasdrubal the Fair governs by diplomacy, and then the army acclaims the young Hannibal. What is at stake is whether one family can build, far from home, the instrument to bring down Rome.

bridge: Chapter 5 built the weapon. Out of the silver mines of Iberia, the Barcid family forged a professional army loyal to itself, and command passed to Hannibal Barca, who had sworn eternal enmity to Rome at nine years old. In 219 BCE he destroyed the Roman-allied city of Saguntum, Rome demanded he be handed over, Carthage refused, and the Romans let fall war. Then Hannibal did the thing nobody expected: rather than fight in Spain or Africa, where Carthage always lost, he resolved to march overland and take the war into Italy itself.
setup: In late October 218 BCE Hannibal leads roughly 50,000 infantry, 9,000 cavalry, and 37 war elephants over the Alps — a crossing of about fifteen days that costs him nearly half his army to rockslides, snow, and hostile mountain tribes before he fights a single battle. What follows is the campaign that fills the military academies. At Trebia and at Lake Trasimene he destroys Roman armies whole; then, on a flat plain at Cannae in 216 BCE, he executes the double envelopment that annihilates the largest army Rome had ever raised — the gold standard of tactical destruction, never improved on since. By any normal logic of ancient war, this should end it. Instead Rome does the most remarkable thing in its military history: it simply refuses to negotiate, raises new armies, and grinds Hannibal down. The question this chapter settles is whether the greatest field commander of the ancient world can actually win the war he keeps winning the battles of.

bridge: The last five chapters followed Carthage through its wars — the rise to mastery of the sea, the African empire, and the two existential struggles with Rome that ended Hannibal undefeated in battle yet beaten at Zama. But the wars are only what Carthage's enemies bothered to record in detail. This chapter steps off the battlefield to ask who these people actually were, because in 146 BCE Rome would burn every word the Carthaginians wrote about themselves, leaving us to reconstruct a whole civilization from its enemies' notes and what the dirt preserved.
setup: This is the cultural portrait — the gods, the money, the military system, and the one Carthaginian voice that survived. The religion centered on Baal Hammon and the rising goddess Tanit, and it leads straight back to the fiercest question in Punic studies: the Tophet, with its thousands of urns of cremated infants. Were these child sacrifices, as the hostile Greek and Roman sources unanimously claim, or a sacred burial ground for children who died young in a world of brutal infant mortality? The honest answer is that the evidence is genuinely ambiguous and the scholars genuinely divided — and the cruelest part is that the one people who could have told us left no surviving account. The economy is easier: purple dye, grain, Saharan gold, Atlantic tin, the best navigators in the Mediterranean. The army is easier still, because Carthage outsourced its fighting to foreign mercenaries and its enemies described them obsessively. And one voice did escape the silence — a Carthaginian-born playwright who became one of Rome's greatest, writing only in his conquerors' tongue.

bridge: Chapter 6 ended the Second Punic War with Hannibal beaten at Zama and Carthage stripped of its fleet, its overseas empire, and its right to wage war without Rome's permission. Chapter 7 showed the civilization behind those wars — its gods, its trade, its mercenary armies. Now both threads converge on the ending. The peace was designed to keep Carthage permanently subordinate, with Rome's ally Masinissa of Numidia installed as a watchdog free to encroach on Carthaginian land while Carthage could not legally fight back. For fifty years it worked. And then Carthage did the one thing Rome could not forgive: it prospered.
setup: Disarmed and defanged, Carthage recovers so fast that by the 190s BCE it offers to pay off its entire fifty-year debt early — and Rome, unwilling to lose the leverage, declines. That prosperity terrifies a faction led by the old senator Cato the Elder, who ends every Senate speech, whatever the topic, with the same words: Carthage must be destroyed. In 149 BCE Rome manufactures its pretext, demands first all of Carthage's weapons and then that the entire maritime city abandon the coast and resettle ten miles inland — a death sentence for a civilization built around the sea. Carthage, already disarmed, decides to fight anyway: workshops become weapons factories, women cut their hair for bowstrings, and a three-year siege begins. What is at stake is no longer power or territory but survival itself — and behind the fire, the deeper question this whole book has circled: what happens to a people when the winners of history burn their books.
